questions.stem: What kind of dependency does Second Normal Form (2NF) eliminate?
options: Partial dependencies
Transitive dependencies
Multi-valued dependencies
Join dependencies
Domain dependencies
questions.explanation: 2NF builds on 1NF by eliminating partial dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite primary key.

questions.stem: Which two conditions must a table satisfy to be in Second Normal Form?
options: It has a surrogate key and no foreign keys
It is already in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the entire primary key
It is in 3NF and every determinant is a superkey
It has no repeating groups and no transitive dependencies
It has a single-column key and atomic values
questions.explanation: A table is in 2NF if it is already in First Normal Form and every non-key attribute depends on the entire primary key, not just part of it.

questions.stem: When does the Second Normal Form rule become relevant?
options: Only when a table has more than one foreign key
Only when a table contains repeating groups
Only when a table has a composite primary key
Only when a table has a surrogate key
Only when a table stores historical data
questions.explanation: Partial dependencies can only occur when the primary key is made up of more than one column, so 2NF is relevant only for tables with a composite key.

options: An attribute that depends on another non-key attribute
An attribute that determines a candidate key
An attribute that can hold more than one value
An attribute that depends on only part of a composite key rather than the whole key
An attribute that is optional and may be null
questions.explanation: A partial dependency occurs when an attribute depends on only part of a composite key rather than the whole key, introducing redundancy and update anomalies.

questions.stem: In a repayment table keyed by (LoanID, RepayDate), why does storing LoanAmount violate Second Normal Form?
options: Because LoanAmount is a multi-valued attribute
Because LoanAmount depends on RepayDate alone
Because LoanAmount is a transitive attribute of CustomerName
Because LoanAmount is not atomic
Because LoanAmount depends only on LoanID, not on the full composite key
questions.explanation: LoanAmount is not specific to an individual repayment date; it depends only on LoanID, which is a partial dependency on the composite key.

questions.stem: What practical problem arises when LoanAmount is stored alongside every repayment record?
options: The same loan amount repeats for every repayment row and a correction requires multiple updates
The repayment rows can no longer be uniquely identified
The loan amount becomes a multi-valued attribute
The composite key stops being unique
The repayment date must be stored as text
questions.explanation: Storing LoanAmount with each repayment repeats the value across rows, so if the amount needs correction multiple rows must be updated.

questions.stem: How does Second Normal Form resolve a partial dependency in the loan approval example?
options: By merging the Loan and Repayment tables into one
By moving attributes that depend only on LoanID into a Loan table and keeping repayment-specific attributes in the Repayment table
By replacing the composite key with a single surrogate key
By deleting the LoanAmount attribute entirely
By converting repayment rows into a repeating group
questions.explanation: 2NF separates attributes by dependency: loan information lives in the Loan table and repayment-specific information stays in the Repayment table.

questions.stem: Which issue does Second Normal Form NOT address?
options: Attributes depending on only part of a composite key
Redundancy caused by repeating loan attributes across repayment rows
A non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute
Correct dependency structure against the whole key
Update anomalies caused by partial dependencies
questions.explanation: 2NF concerns itself only with partial dependencies; transitive dependencies, where a non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute, are handled in Third Normal Form.

questions.stem: According to the rule for achieving Second Normal Form, what should be done with an attribute that depends on only part of the key?
options: Mark it as a candidate key
Store it as a comma-separated list
Make it part of the composite key
Move it into a separate table where it fully depends on that table's primary key
Leave it in place and add an index
questions.explanation: The 2NF rule is to examine each non-key attribute of a composite-key table and move any partially dependent attribute into a separate table where it fully depends on that table's key.

questions.stem: What refinement does the move from First to Second Normal Form represent?
options: A move from relational to document storage
A move from atomic values to summary values
A move from a single table to a star schema
A move from transactional to analytical design
A move from merely ensuring atomic values to ensuring correct dependency structure
questions.explanation: The transition to 2NF is a refinement in logical precision: instead of only atomic values, the model now ensures correct dependency structure so each table represents a single concept more cleanly.
